content: The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) has established specific guidelines to manage heat exposure in the workplace. These guidelines aim to prevent acute and chronic heat-related illnesses, unsafe behaviors induced by heat, and harmful interactions between excessive heat and toxic chemicals or physical agents. The recommendations are based on validated and reproducible techniques and are subject to periodic review and revision. Definitions: 1. Acclimatization to Heat: This refers to the physiological and psychological adjustments that occur during the first week of exposure to a hot environment. These adaptations enable an individual to work in such conditions with reduced strain. 2. Unimpaired Mental Performance: This is the ability of an employee to maintain constant alertness and make critical decisions, fine discriminations, or rapid, skillful actions in environments where safety and health depend on such capabilities. 3. Intermittent Heat Exposure: This involves exposure to hot conditions for no longer than 15 minutes, followed by intervals in a cooler environment, either spontaneously or as per a prescribed schedule. 4. Continuous Heat Exposure: This refers to any exposure to hot conditions that does not meet the criteria for intermittent exposure. 5. Hot Environmental Conditions: These are defined as any combination of air temperature, humidity, radiation, and wind speed that exceeds a Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) of 79°F. Applicability: The standard applies to all workplaces, both indoor and outdoor, and to all employees, except those required to wear impermeable protective clothing. Acclimatization Protocol: 1. For Unacclimatized Employees: A six-day acclimatization schedule is required, starting with 50% of the anticipated workload and exposure time on the first day, increasing by 10% daily until reaching 100% on the sixth day. 2. For Regularly Acclimatized Employees Returning After Absence: Employees returning after nine or more consecutive days of leave must undergo a four-day acclimatization period, starting with 50% exposure on the first day and increasing by 20% daily until reaching 100% on the fourth day. 3. For Employees Returning After Illness: Employees returning after four consecutive days of illness must have medical clearance and follow the same four-day acclimatization schedule. Work Practices: 1. A work-rest regimen should be implemented to reduce physiological strain and improve recovery during rest periods. 2. Workload should be evenly distributed throughout the workday whenever possible. 3. Hot jobs should be scheduled during the coolest part of the work shift when feasible. 4. Regular breaks, at least one per hour, should be provided for water and salt replacement. Employees should have access to either 1% salted drinking water or a minimum of 8 quarts of cool potable water and salt tablets per shift. Water supplies should be located within 200 feet of the work area. 5. Appropriate protective clothing and equipment must be provided and used. 6. Engineering controls, such as ventilation or cooling systems, should be utilized to reduce environmental heat load. Monitoring Heat Exposure: 1. For continuous exposure, the WBGT should be calculated as an hourly time-weighted average. 2. For intermittent exposure, the WBGT should be calculated as a two-hour time-weighted average. Medical Evaluations: 1. Employees aged 45 or older with no prior occupational heat exposure should not be assigned to jobs with environmental conditions exceeding 79°F WBGT for men and 76°F WBGT for women until they are acclimatized. 2. All employees assigned to hot jobs for the first time must undergo a medical evaluation to ensure they can cope with the hot environment. The evaluation should emphasize the cardiovascular, renal, hepatic, endocrine, respiratory systems, and skin, along with a complete medical history focusing on previous heat-related disorders. 3. Periodic physical examinations should be conducted every two years for employees under 45 and annually for those aged 45 or older. These exams should include all components of the pre-placement evaluation. Education and Training: Employees should be educated on: The importance of water and salt intake for replacement purposes. The significance of daily weight monitoring before and after work. Recognizing symptoms of heat disorders, including dehydration, heat exhaustion, heat syncope, heat cramps, salt deficiency exhaustion, prickly heat, and heat stroke. Special precautions for situations involving exposure to toxic agents or other physical stressors in addition to heat. The process and benefits of heat acclimatization. Warning Signs: Warning signs must be placed in areas where environmental conditions reach or exceed 86°F WBGT to alert individuals entering such zones. Recordkeeping: 1. Records of acclimatization schedules and WBGT measurements for each work area must be maintained for the duration of the employee's employment and for one year thereafter. 2. These records should be readily accessible to workers and maintained as per the guidelines set by the Secretary of Labor in consultation with the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare. Observations on Heat Stress: Workers in hot jobs often self-select based on their ability to tolerate heat, leading to a population with high physical performance and adaptability. Heat disorders are more likely to occur during the first hot spell of summer, after weekends or vacations, or following illness when workers are unacclimatized or less physically fit. Dehydration is common among workers in hot environments due to insufficient water intake relative to sweat loss. This can be mitigated by providing accessible, high-quality drinking water and encouraging frequent, small water intakes. Historical and Epidemiological Insights: Early studies on heat stress, such as those on Cornish tin miners, highlighted the health risks of hot working environments. Chronic heat exposure can lead to serious health and safety consequences, including increased morbidity and mortality rates, particularly in industries with inadequate medical examinations and fitness standards. Acute effects of heat include increased accident rates, often due to reduced alertness, irritation, and emotional disturbances caused by high temperatures. Preventive Measures: Pre-placement and periodic medical examinations, acclimatization programs, and monitoring of oral temperature and heart rate are essential. Modifications to reduce heat stress may include engineering controls, protective clothing, and adjustments to work schedules and workloads. Workers should be educated on the importance of hydration and salt intake, and supervisors must ensure access to water and rest breaks. By implementing these measures, the health and safety of workers in hot environments can be significantly improved, reducing the risk of heat-related illnesses and maintaining optimal work efficiency.
